transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I guess they sent me from the station. It wasn’t—people keep saying I was “not listening,” but the airway bags were wrong, the way they were sitting. I had to move them into the right pattern, and the dispatch numbers, I was saying them out loud because if you don’t keep the sequence then things... the whole bay feels like it can turn bad.

My lieutenant told me to stop, but I couldn’t just step away in the middle of it. It’s like leaving a stretcher half-locked, you know? Except everyone was staring, and then it became about me instead of the bags.
When this happens, do you feel like the need to arrange things and repeat the numbers is unreasonable or excessive?

I don’t know if “unreasonable” is the right word. It didn’t feel that way at the time. It felt necessary, like when you check a rig and something is off by just one thing and everybody acts like you’re being picky, but then later that one thing matters.

The airway bags were not sitting right, so I kept moving them into the pattern I knew was right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud to keep the sequence. My lieutenant told me to stop, but I couldn’t just walk away from it. If I broke it, the whole bay felt like it could go bad.
Do you believe that if the bags are not in that exact pattern, something bad really will happen?

I mean… yeah, in that moment it felt real. Not like I was trying to be difficult. The bags had to be in the right pattern, and the dispatch numbers had to stay in order, out loud, because if I broke it or stepped away when my lieutenant told me to stop, it felt like the whole bay could go bad.

It’s hard to explain because it sounds stupid when I say it here, but at the station, with everyone moving around and the radios going, it was like… you don’t leave something half-done. You don’t leave a rig wrong. So I kept fixing it.
When this is happening, does it feel like the idea about the pattern is coming from your own mind, or like it is being put into your mind from outside?

I don’t know. I mean, it feels like… it’s just there, like when you walk into a room and you know something is off before you know what it is. I don’t sit down and decide it, if that’s what you mean.

But “outside” is a weird word. Outside like the radio? Because at the station the radio is always going, and dispatch tones get stuck in your head, and then you’re counting them, and then somebody drops a clipboard or starts talking about lunch like nothing is happening. I used to have a partner who would leave the monitor cables all twisted, drove me crazy, because then on a call you’re fighting the cables instead of the patient.

So… I’m not sure how to answer. It feels like it’s in my head, but not like a normal thought I can just put down.
When you’re calm and away from the station, do you think the bay would really go bad if the bags weren’t in that exact pattern?

When I’m away from there, calm… I can sort of hear how it sounds. Like, no, a bag being two inches off shouldn’t make the whole bay go bad. I know that sitting here.

But at the station it wasn’t like that. They sent me here because I kept moving the airway bags into the pattern that felt right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over, to keep it straight. My lieutenant told me to step away, and I couldn’t. It felt like if I broke the sequence, something in the bay would go wrong.

It’s like when the coffee pot’s left on overnight—sorry, that’s not the same thing, but the whole place has these little things people ignore until they become a problem. So calm, away from it, I can say it probably doesn’t make sense. But when I’m there, it feels real.
When the urge to arrange the bags or repeat the numbers starts, do you try to resist it?

I try to, yeah… or I think I’m trying to. My lieutenant was telling me to step away, and I knew I was supposed to just stop, but I kept going back to the airway bags, moving them into the pattern that felt right.

And the dispatch numbers, I kept saying them out loud, like if I could keep the order then everything would be okay. It’s not like I wanted to stand there making everyone mad. It just felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad.

The station gets like that sometimes, you know, everything in its place, and then someone leaves something half-done and later it turns into a mess. But… yeah, I couldn’t really resist it then. I wouldn’t step away when he told me to.
Right now, do you believe the bags really have to be in that exact pattern to prevent something bad from happening?

Right now… sitting here, I can say it sounds extreme. Like, bags are bags, they shouldn’t control the whole station.

But when I was there, that’s why they sent me here. I kept moving the airway bags back into the pattern because I knew that was the right way, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud to keep it lined up. My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, and I just… I couldn’t do it. It felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad.

The bay has a rhythm, you know? If one thing is off, then the next thing is off, and then someone’s looking for a mask or a cable and—sorry. But yes, in that moment it really felt like it had to be that exact pattern.
Do these urges to arrange the bags and repeat the numbers feel unwanted to you?

Unwanted… yeah, I mean, I didn’t want to be doing it, not like that. I wasn’t trying to make a scene.

They sent me here because I kept moving the airway bags into that pattern I knew was right, and I kept repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, and my lieutenant told me to stop, to step away, and I just couldn’t. It felt like if I stopped—if I broke the sequence—the whole bay would go bad.

It’s strange because part of me hates it. Like when you’re checking the rig and somebody’s moved one little thing, and then you think about the last call where something wasn’t where it should’ve been… but that’s not exactly what you asked. The urge feels unwanted, yes, but also like I have to do it anyway.
When this is happening, do you think your fear that the bay will go bad is probably true, or probably not true?

Probably true when I’m in it. I mean… sitting here I can hear how that sounds, but at the station it didn’t feel like a “probably.” It felt like I knew the airway bags had to be in that pattern, and I kept saying the dispatch numbers out loud to keep things lined up.

My lieutenant was telling me to stop, step away, and I just wouldn’t—couldn’t, I guess. Because if I broke the sequence, it felt like the whole bay would go bad. Like one thing out of place turns into everything out of place, and then everyone acts surprised when the shift falls apart. So… in the moment, yes, I think I believed it was true.
When you’re in the middle of it at the station, are you completely convinced something bad will happen if you don’t do it?

Yeah… when I’m in the middle of it, it feels completely true. Not like I’m weighing it out like, “maybe this is silly.” It’s more like the bay has already started going wrong if I don’t fix it.

That’s why they sent me here. I kept moving the airway bags back into the pattern I knew was right, and I was saying the dispatch numbers out loud, because the numbers kind of… keep the order, if that makes sense. My lieutenant kept telling me to stop and step away, and I heard him, but I couldn’t make myself do it.

I know people say “nothing would happen,” but right then it felt like if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. Like, not just messy—bad. So yes, in that moment I’m convinced.
